summary: Analyzes approaches ISPs can take to manage the IP6.ARPA reverse DNS zone. In IPv4 ISPs often pre-populate one PTR record per address, which does not scale in IPv6.

eli5.summary: There are too many IPv6 addresses to write a name for each one. This talks about better ways to do it.

questions: how do isps manage reverse dns in ipv6
subtitle: Practical approaches for Internet Service Providers to manage reverse DNS lookups in IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: In IPv4, ISPs pre-populate the reverse DNS zone (IN-ADDR.ARPA) with one PTR record per address. This approach does not scale in IPv6, where a single /48 prefix contains 2^80 possible addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC analyzes five practical alternatives: negative responses, wildcard records, dynamic DNS updates, delegated zones, and on-the-fly PTR generation. Each trades off simplicity, accuracy, and scalability.
tldr.outcome: ISPs now have guidance on choosing an approach suited to their network size and requirements, though no single approach is optimal for all situations.

facts.label: Time to create all records at 1000/sec

today: RFC 8501 is an Informational specification that provides practical guidance for ISPs deploying IPv6. While there is no recommended standard approach, ISPs generally adopt a method suited to their customer base: residential ISPs often use dynamic generation or wildcards, while commercial ISPs may delegate zones to customers capable of managing DNS.

sections.title: The Reverse DNS Problem in IPv6
sections.content:
In IPv4, an Internet Service Provider typically owns a block of addresses (such as 192.0.2.0/24) and populates the reverse DNS zone (IN-ADDR.ARPA) with one PTR record for each address. This allows reverse lookups to return a hostname.

IPv6 changes the scale dramatically. When an ISP delegates a /48 prefix to a customer, that prefix contains 2^80 possible addresses. Writing one record per address is impractical: at 1,000 entries per second, it would take 38 trillion years to complete the zone. Additionally, many IPv6 hosts use Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), which generates their own addresses randomly, making it impossible for the ISP to know all addresses in advance.
sections.eli5: In IPv4, you name a few hundred addresses. In IPv6, you could have trillions. The old way does not work.

sections.title: Alternative Approaches to Reverse DNS
sections.content:
This RFC describes five approaches that ISPs can choose from, each with different trade-offs:

Negative Response: Return NXDOMAIN (no such domain) to PTR queries. This is accurate because the ISP does not maintain a name for each address, but some services rely on successful DNS lookups and may have a poor experience.

Wildcard Records: Create one wildcard PTR record per customer prefix. This scales well but does not allow a forward lookup to return the same hostname, violating the expectation that forward and reverse DNS match.

Dynamic DNS: Allow hosts or gateways to update DNS records dynamically after configuring their address. This maintains matching forward and reverse records but requires host support and introduces security risks from unsecured updates.

Delegate DNS: For customers capable of running their own DNS servers, delegate the reverse zone to them. This works well for commercial customers but is impractical for residential ISPs.

Dynamic Generation: Generate PTR records on the fly when requested, using an algorithm to create matching forward and reverse records. This is simple and scalable but requires the same algorithm on all servers.
sections.eli5: Five choices: say 'no record', use wildcards, let customers update it, let them run DNS, or make it up when someone asks.

sections.title: Dynamic DNS Options in Detail
sections.content:
Dynamic DNS has several sub-approaches. In the simplest case, individual hosts update DNS directly after autoconfiguring an address, using the ISP's provided DNS search list to form a qualified name. This requires hosts to be configured for dynamic DNS, which is not default behavior.

Residential gateways can be configured as intermediaries, accepting DHCP requests from local hosts and updating DNS on their behalf. Or the ISP can delegate the reverse zone to customer gateways capable of running authoritative name servers; however, most residential users lack equipment or expertise for this.

The ISP's DHCP server can automatically populate DNS when processing a DHCP request, if the request contains hostname information. Similarly, the ISP's RADIUS server can populate DNS from accounting records of allocated addresses and prefixes.
sections.eli5: You can have individual computers update DNS, a home router update on their behalf, or the ISP automatically update DNS from DHCP or RADIUS records.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Concerns
sections.content:
Dynamic DNS introduces security risks. Without authentication, malicious users can inject false PTR records. The RFC recommends using TSIG (Transaction Signatures) for authenticated updates or at least ingress filtering to accept updates only from customer address space. ISPs should rate-limit updates to prevent denial-of-service attacks.

Privacy is a concern with user-updated records. An ISP that allows dynamic DNS should consider that users might create hostnames revealing sensitive information, such as hostnames describing medical conditions or personal details.

On-the-fly generation may expose infrastructure details if the algorithm can be reverse-engineered. DNSSEC signing of dynamically generated records increases server load.
sections.eli5: If users update DNS, they might put private information in hostnames. Servers also need protection from fake updates and attacks.
